finding.claim: Broken access control: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result, so no authorization is enforced. Any user who can reach the route can overwrite the body of any document. The sibling handler update_title correctly uses require_edit().
finding.source: Authenticated but unauthorized user (g.user) sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...} for a doc they neither own nor edit.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (write to the document body)

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> entry; doc_id is attacker-controlled
doc loaded by id with no ownership scoping
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns bool, result ignored, so no abort(403)

finding.guards_checked: can_edit at line 19 is called but its return value is unused. require_edit (lines 11-13), which aborts with 403, is not called here. No other middleware or before_request auth exists in the file. The sibling route /doc/<doc_id>/title at line 27 does enforce it, so this is the missing-check outlier.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit (docs.py:7-8) returns a bool that is discarded at line 19; require_edit (docs.py:11-13) aborts but is not called in update_doc; no before_request or decorator auth exists in the file.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit() as a bare statement and discards the bool, so docs.py:20 overwrites the body for any authenticated user, whereas update_title uses require_edit at docs.py:27. The only part of the finding I couldn't see is how g.user gets set, since no auth code is in the file.
